youtube.title: C++ Encapsulation: Getters, Setters and Safe Data | C++ Programming EP 56
youtube.description: In this episode you will hide data and offer safe functions, validate input in a setter and keep a class in a valid state, with Xecxec the crab. 0:00 Intro · 0:15 Encapsulation · 1:13 A safe account · 2:07 Checked access · 2:43 Second program · 3:45 Recap · 4:15 Bug of the Day · 5:06 Challenge · 5:32 Next episode

thumbnail.pose: Xecxec next to a bank vault with a small window for deposits

scenes.animation: Tomato title card: EP sticker thuds in, title stamps with a whoosh, Xecxec scuttles in and waves; thud, whoosh, claw-click, sting
scenes.narration: Today we see why classes hide their data. The class checks every change, so it never ends up in a bad state.

scenes.onScreen: "Encapsulation": numbered lines (1. Keep data private; 2. Offer public functions that check the input; 3. The class keeps itself valid) and an analogy card: a bank counter: you cannot reach the vault, but the clerk checks every deposit
scenes.animation: Lines spring in one by one with a pop; the analogy card slides in from the right
scenes.narration: Encapsulation means hiding the data and offering checked functions. A setter can refuse a bad value. A getter lets others read the value. Then the class always stays valid. Think of a bank counter. You cannot reach the vault, but the clerk checks every deposit. Encapsulation protects the rules of your class. If the balance is a public number, any code can set it to minus a million. If the balance is private, only the class decides what is allowed. A good class is easy to use and hard to misuse. Keep the data private, and keep the functions few.
points: Offer public functions that check the input

analogy.title: Encapsulation
analogy.body: A bank counter: you cannot reach the vault, but the clerk checks every deposit

scenes.onScreen: account.cpp: deposit refuses a negative amount
scenes.animation: Code types in with key-tick; butter [HL n] highlight sweeps line by line with marker-swipe; explanation card on the right
scenes.narration: [HL 5] The balance is private. [HL 8] Deposit is the only way to add money. [HL 9] It refuses an amount of zero or less. [HL 12] A good amount is added. [HL 20] Main deposits five hundred. [HL 21] Then it tries to deposit minus twenty. The answer is false. [HL 22] The balance is still five hundred. [HL 5] The balance is private, and it starts at zero. [HL 9] The deposit function checks the amount first. A zero or negative amount is refused. [HL 12] Only a good amount reaches the balance. [HL 21] The deposit of minus twenty fails, so the output is false. [HL 22] The balance stays five hundred.

scenes.onScreen: a flow: call, check, change or refuse
scenes.animation: Steps drop in left to right with a pop; connecting arrows draw on; the active step glows butter
scenes.narration: Follow the call. Deposit receives minus twenty. The check finds a bad amount. The function refuses, and returns false. The balance never changes. The outside code cannot break the rule. Notice the guard at the door. Every change goes through a function that checks it. The class can promise that its balance is never below zero, because it has full control.

diagram.caption: a flow: call, check, change or refuse

scenes.onScreen: getset.cpp: a setter that keeps age in range
scenes.animation: Second program or a twist on the first; [HL n] and [TRACK name=value] cues drive the variable tracker; output panel fills line by line with a ding per line
scenes.narration: [HL 8] The getter reads the age. [HL 9] The setter checks the range. [HL 10] Only an age from zero to one hundred twenty is accepted. [HL 18] Seventeen is accepted. [HL 19] Five hundred is refused. [HL 20] The age is still seventeen. [HL 8] The getter returns the age and does not change anything, so it is const. [HL 10] The setter accepts only ages from zero to one hundred and twenty. [HL 19] An age of five hundred is refused, so the age stays at seventeen.

scenes.animation: Dark-blue terminal: the compile command types with key-tick, the run command types, output prints in mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Save the file as getset dot cpp. Compile it with g plus plus. Then run the program. The program prints seventeen. The output is seventeen. The bad value never entered the object.

scenes.animation: Recap lines tick in one by one with a pop; Xecxec nods after each tick
scenes.narration: Let us recap. One. Keep data private. Two. Offer public functions that check the input. Three. A setter can refuse a bad value. Four. The class always stays in a valid state. Pause the video. Say these ideas out loud, one time, slowly.
points: Offer public functions that check the input.
A setter can refuse a bad value.
The class always stays in a valid state.

scenes.onScreen: BUG OF THE DAY: A setter that does not check
scenes.animation: Butter banner drops in with a buzzer; the program runs and the wrong output appears in tomato; the fix slides in and the output turns mint with a ding
scenes.narration: Bug of the Day. The setter stores any number. The program prints an age of minus five. The data is private, but the setter gives no protection. Add a check, so that the class stays valid. A setter that stores any value gives no protection at all. It is a public field with extra typing. Add a check in the setter. Then the class can promise that its data always follows the rules.

scenes.onScreen: Task card: write a safe class
scenes.animation: Task card pops in; checklist ticks with a pop; Xecxec holds a tiny pen
scenes.narration: Your challenge: Write a Thermostat class. The setter must accept only temperatures from ten to thirty degrees. Hint: the setter tests that the value is at least ten and at most thirty, and stores it only then. Write your answer in the comments.

scenes.narration: Next time: this and const methods. Keep coding, says Xecxec!

bug.error:
Program output (it runs, but the answer is wrong):

-5
bug.why: A setter without a check is the same as a public field. The age of minus five breaks the rules of the class.

pun: "The vault told the thief, you can only deposit your complaints at the window."
challenge: Write a Thermostat class. The setter must accept only temperatures from ten to thirty degrees. Hint: the setter tests that the value is at least ten and at most thirty, and stores it only then.
challengeAnswer: Keep the temperature private. In the setter, test that the value is at least ten and at most thirty. Store it only then.
